accelerators.source: Vendor datasheets/architecture pages, retrieved 2026-09: NVIDIA H200 datasheet (BF16 1,979 / FP8 3,958 TFLOPS sparse, 141 GB HBM3e, 4.8 TB/s, 900 GB/s NVLink, up to 700 W); NVIDIA H100 tensor-core GPU datasheet (dense BF16 989 / dense FP8 1,979, 80 GB HBM3, 3.35 TB/s, 900 GB/s NVLink, up to 700 W); NVIDIA A100 80GB datasheet (dense BF16/FP16 312, 80 GB HBM2e, 2,039 GB/s, 600 GB/s NVLink, 400 W; no FP8/FP4 tensor support); NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 page (72 Blackwell GPUs, 13.4 TB HBM3E at 576 TB/s aggregate, NVFP4 1,440 / FP8 720 / FP16-BF16 360 PFLOPS sparse, 130 TB/s NVLink, ~120 kW liquid-cooled rack); NVIDIA Blackwell architecture (B200 192 GB HBM3e, 8 TB/s, 2,250 dense BF16 / 4,500 dense FP8 / 9,000 dense FP4 TFLOPS, 1.8 TB/s NVLink, 1,000 W). AMD Instinct MI300X product page (192 GB HBM3, 5,325 GB/s, dense BF16/FP16 1,307 / dense FP8 2,615 TFLOPS, 8 Infinity Fabric links x 128 GB/s, 750 W; no native FP4). Google Cloud TPU v5e docs (16 GB HBM, 800 GiB/s, 197 BF16 / 393 INT8 TFLOPs, 400 GB/s ICI) and TPU v5p docs (95 GB HBM, 2,765 GB/s, 459 BF16 / 459 FP8 TFLOPs, 1,200 GB/s ICI). AWS EC2 Trn2 product page (trn2.48xlarge = 16 Trainium2 chips, 20.8 FP8 PFLOPS, 1.5 TB HBM3, 46 TB/s aggregate => ~1.3 PFLOPS FP8, ~650 dense BF16, 96 GB HBM3 and ~2.9 TB/s per chip). Caveat: NVIDIA headlines (H100/H200/B200/GB200) are quoted WITH 2:4 sparsity, so the dense bf16TFLOPs/fp8TFLOPs/fp4TFLOPs here are half the headline; AMD and Google quote dense directly. Trainium2 per-chip BF16 is derived as half of the published FP8 rate and is approximate. 'null' means the format is not natively supported.

model_configs.source: Official model configs and technical reports. Llama 3.1 8B/70B/405B: Meta Llama 3.1 model card and Hugging Face config.json (32/80/126 layers, hidden 4,096/8,192/16,384, 32/64/128 heads, 8 KV heads, head_dim 128, GQA, 128K context; 8.03B / 70.6B / 405B parameters). DeepSeek-V3: DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report, arXiv:2412.19437 (27 Dec 2024) and Hugging Face deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V3 config.json (61 layers, hidden 7,168, 128 heads, MLA with kv_lora_rank 512, 671B total / 37B active, config max_position_embeddings 163,840 while 128K is the advertised context). Kimi K2: Moonshot AI Kimi-K2-Instruct config.json (61 layers, hidden 7,168, 64 heads, MLA, 384 routed experts, 8 active + 1 shared, ~1T total / 32B active, 131,072 context). Mistral 7B: mistralai/Mistral-7B-v0.1 config.json (32 layers, hidden 4,096, 32 heads, 8 KV heads, head_dim 128, sliding_window 4,096, 7.24B params, 32,768 context). gpt-oss-120b: openai/gpt-oss-120b config.json (36 layers, hidden 2,880, 64 heads, 8 KV heads, head_dim 64, 128 experts with 4 active, alternating sliding/full attention, ~117B total / ~5.1B active, 131,072 context). Parameter counts for Llama 3.1 are the commonly cited rounded figures rather than exact config-derived totals.

kv_scheme_savings.source: Computed from the official configs in model_configs (formula: bytes/token = 2 x layers x n_kv_heads x d_head x 2 bytes for FP16 K and V). MHA/GQA/MQA/SWA use Llama-3-70B geometry (80 layers, 64 query heads, head_dim 128, 8 KV heads for GQA); MLA uses DeepSeek-V3 geometry (61 layers, kv_lora_rank 512 + qk_rope_head_dim 64 = 576 cached elements per layer per token, from DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report arXiv:2412.19437, which states MLA compresses the KV cache to a latent vector). These are per-token, whole-model figures; real engines add paging and block overhead. Ratios are arithmetic from these geometries and will differ for other models.

items.note: Llama-3-70B-class geometry: 80 layers x 64 KV heads x 128 dim x 2 (K,V) x 2 bytes = 2.62 MB/token. MHA caches grown for every head.
8 KV heads instead of 64; used by Llama 3.1, Mistral 7B and gpt-oss-120b. 0.33 MB/token at this geometry.
Single KV head; 0.04 MB/token. Rare in frontier models because quality can suffer.

items.savingVsMHA: about 57x vs MHA at the same 61-layer/128-head geometry
items.note: DeepSeek-V3 caches a 512-element latent plus a 64-element RoPE key per layer: 61 x 576 x 2 bytes = 0.07 MB/token. DeepSeek's own MHA equivalent (61 x 128 heads x 128 dim) would be ~4.0 MB/token.

items.savingVsMHA: 8x per token vs MHA, plus a hard cap from the sliding window
items.note: Mistral 7B geometry (32 layers, 8 KV heads) = 0.13 MB/token, but the cache stops growing past the 4,096-token sliding window, so peak memory is bounded rather than linear in sequence length.

disaggregation.source: DistServe (Zhong et al., OSDI 2024, arXiv:2401.09670, Jan 2024) reports serving 7.4x more requests or 12.6x tighter SLO by splitting prefill and decode. DeepSeek's 'DeepSeek-V3/R1 Inference System Overview' (github.com/deepseek-ai/open-infra-index, 2025-02-28) publishes the prefill/decode node split (Routed Expert EP32 prefill, EP144 decode) and the 24-hour service totals of 608B input and 168B output tokens. Mooncake (arXiv:2407.00079, Qin et al.) describes Kimi/Moonshot's KVCache-centric disaggregated serving and reports up to 525% throughput in simulation and 75% more real requests. Caveat: the value 20 in distServeSpeedups is a broadly cited upper-end 'goodput' figure for disaggregated deployments; the DistServe paper itself reports 7.4x/12.6x, so 20 is a rounded composite, not a single published measurement. The 100B tokens/day for Kimi is an approximate, widely repeated service-scale figure that varies by source and date and is not stated verbatim in the Mooncake paper; treat it as indicative.

deepseek.note: Per deployment unit on H800 GPUs: prefill spans 4 nodes with EP32 (32 GPUs), decode spans 18 nodes with EP144 (144 GPUs). Totals are for all V3/R1 traffic over 24h (UTC+8 2025-02-27 12:00 to 2025-02-28 12:00); 342B of the 608B input tokens (56.3%) hit the on-disk KV cache. Average decode speed was 20-22 tokens/s.

prefix_cache.source: RadixAttention: SGLang paper (Zheng et al., arXiv:2312.07104), which reports up to 6.4x higher throughput than prior systems; the 6.0 here is a rounded conservative value. vLLM x Mooncake: vLLM blog 'Serving Agentic Workloads at Scale with vLLM x Mooncake' (vllm.ai/blog/2026-05-06-mooncake-store, 6 May 2026) and the Mooncake benchmark site, reporting 3.8x higher throughput and 46x lower P50 TTFT (and 8.6x lower end-to-end latency) on realistic Codex agentic traces with 12 GB200 GPUs, driven by cache hit rate rising from 1.7% to 92.2%. Tier latency: these are order-of-magnitude, guide-friendly approximations consistent with the well-known memory/tier latency tables popularised by Jeff Dean and Colin Scott's 'Latency Numbers Every Programmer Should Know' and with NVMe/network round-trip figures; they are illustrative, not a single published benchmark, and real remote-tier latency depends heavily on interconnect and fabric.

speculative.source: Medusa (Cai et al., arXiv:2401.10774, Jan 2024): Medusa-1 >2.2x and Medusa-2 2.3-3.6x lossless. EAGLE-2 (Li et al., arXiv:2406.16858, Jun 2024): 3.05x-4.26x, 20-40% faster than EAGLE-1. EAGLE-3 (Li et al., arXiv:2503.01840, Mar 2025): up to 6.5x, ~1.4x over EAGLE-2, and 1.38x throughput at batch 64 in SGLang. Draft-model speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., arXiv:2211.17192, ICML 2023): 2x-3x on T5-XXL with identical outputs. N-gram/prompt-lookup: the technique is documented in vLLM's speculative-decoding feature and in Saxena's 'Prompt Lookup Decoding'; gains are highly workload-dependent (near-zero for open-ended chat, high for copy/edit/summarisation). Speedups are paper maxima, not guaranteed production numbers.

items.acceptance: High only when the continuation copies the prompt (summarisation, code edit, RAG); near zero on open-ended chat
items.note: No draft model and no extra parameters; speedup is workload-dependent and can be <1x when hit rate is low.

items.acceptance: Multiple decoding heads verified in parallel; paper reports >2.2x (Medusa-1) and 2.3-3.6x (Medusa-2)
items.note: Adds extra heads to a frozen or jointly fine-tuned backbone; needs fine-tuning.
Lossless; 20-40% faster than EAGLE-1.

items.acceptance: Direct token prediction with multi-layer feature fusion; up to 6.5x, ~1.4x over EAGLE-2
items.note: 1.38x throughput at batch size 64 in SGLang; the 6.5x is a single-request/low-batch maximum.

items.acceptance: Depends on draft/target agreement; 2x-3x on T5-XXL
items.note: Exact (distribution-preserving) but costs extra memory and serves a second model.

quantization.source: GPTQ (Frantar et al., ICLR 2023, arXiv:2210.17323): 3-4 bit weights with negligible degradation and ~3.25x end-to-end speedup on A100. AWQ (Lin et al., MLSys 2024 Best Paper, arXiv:2306.00978): 4-bit weight-only, protects ~1% salient channels, >3x over FP16 on desktop/mobile GPUs. FP8 E4M3 (with per-block scaling) is the native training/inference format of DeepSeek-V3 (DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report arXiv:2412.19437) and of NVIDIA Hopper/Blackwell Tensor Cores; NVIDIA reports near-parity with BF16. NVFP4/MXFP4 are the Blackwell and gpt-oss microscaling 4-bit formats (openai/gpt-oss-120b config.json specifies mxfp4). Accuracy deltas are typical ranges from the cited papers and NVIDIA/community evaluations, not guarantees; weight-only INT4 is usually more benign than INT4 activations. bytesPerParam counts weights only and ignores scales/zero-points and any KV-cache quantization.

items.note: Standard training/inference format on modern accelerators.
Same width; BF16 usually preferred for its wider exponent range.
Native on Hopper/Blackwell and used by DeepSeek-V3. E4M3 for weights/activations with per-block (e.g. 128x128) scaling; E5M2 for some gradients.
Quantizes both weights and activations; needs calibration and good scaling.

items.eval: Perplexity and MMLU within a few points at 4-bit
items.note: Weights only, activations stay FP16. AWQ is usually the safer choice for instruction-tuned models; group size and calibration matter.

items.accuracyDelta: Measurable but often small with block scales
items.eval: Microscaling (MX) block formats; used by gpt-oss-120b and Blackwell
items.note: 4-bit with shared block exponents (NVFP4 adds a per-block FP8 scale). Quality depends heavily on block size and whether sensitive layers (attention, router, embeddings) are kept higher precision.

moe.source: DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report (arXiv:2412.19437, Dec 2024) for the 256 routed + 1 shared expert, 8 active, and the auxiliary-loss-free load-balancing design; DeepSeek-V3/R1 Inference System Overview (open-infra-index, 2025-02-28) for large-scale expert parallelism and the expert-parallel load balancer; deepseek-ai/EPLB README (open source Feb 2025) for redundant-expert replication. The hot-expert statistic 'top 3-5% of experts absorb 30-50% of tokens' is a widely repeated rule-of-thumb that captures a real, well-documented phenomenon (DeepSeek notes 'inherently high-load experts'), but the exact percentages vary by model, dataset and routing scheme, and no single canonical paper states that range; treat it as an approximate, contested illustration. The ~20% EPLB gain is likewise an approximate, commonly cited figure for rebalancing DeepSeek-V3-class expert parallelism and is not a single published measurement.
moe.hotExpertTokenShare: top 3-5% of experts absorb 30-50% of tokens

long_context.source: StreamingLLM (Xiao et al., ICLR 2024, arXiv:2309.17453): stable to 4M tokens and up to 22.2x faster than sliding-window recomputation. H2O (Zhang et al., arXiv:2306.14048): 20% heavy hitters + recent tokens, up to 29x throughput over DeepSpeed/Accelerate baselines and 1.9x lower latency at equal batch. SnapKV (Li et al., arXiv:2404.14469): 3.6x decoding speedup and 8.2x memory efficiency at 16K, up to 380K context on one A100-80GB. PyramidKV (Cai et al., arXiv:2406.02069): matches full cache with 12% of KV and gives 100.0 Needle-in-a-Haystack accuracy for Llama-3-70B with only 128 retained entries. Quest (Tang et al., ICML 2024, arXiv:2406.10774): query-aware top-K pages, up to 7.03x latency reduction / 2.23x self-attention speedup. DuoAttention (Xiao et al., arXiv:2410.10819): full cache for retrieval heads and constant cache for streaming heads, up to 2.55x memory reduction and 2.18x decoding speedup for MHA (1.67x / 1.50x for GQA), 3.3M context for Llama-3-8B on one A100 with quantization. Budgets and speedups are paper-reported maxima and depend on workload, model and hardware.

items.note: KV cache and decode cost grow linearly with sequence length; correctness baseline.

items.qualityRetained: Degrades once the text exceeds W; loses long-range retrieval
items.speedup: Decode cost becomes O(W) instead of O(sequence)
items.note: Used natively by Mistral 7B (window 4,096) and in gpt-oss alternating layers.

items.budget: A few sink tokens + recent window
items.qualityRetained: Stable to 4M+ tokens, but weak on long-range retrieval
items.note: No fine-tuning; keeps the first few tokens as an attention sink.
Dynamic submodular eviction; keep both recent and high-attention tokens.

items.speedup: 3.6x decode, 8.2x memory efficiency at 16K; 380K on one A100-80GB
items.note: Picks important prefix positions using an observation window at the end of the prompt; no fine-tuning.

items.budget: Layer-wise pyramidal budget (more low layers, fewer high layers)
items.qualityRetained: Matches full cache at 12% KV; 100.0 on Needle-in-a-Haystack with 128 entries (Llama-3-70B)
items.speedup: Memory reduction proportional to retained fraction
items.note: Exploits pyramidal information funnelling: attention scatters in low layers and focuses in high layers.

items.budget: Top-K critical KV pages selected per query
items.qualityRetained: Negligible accuracy loss on long-dependency tasks
items.note: Query-aware: tracks min/max key per page to estimate page criticality.

items.budget: Full KV for retrieval heads, constant-length KV for streaming heads
items.note: A small fraction of retrieval heads carry long-range attention; the rest only need recent tokens and sinks.

structured_output.source: XGrammar (Dong et al., MLSys 2025, arXiv:2411.15100, Nov 2024) accelerates context-free-grammar constrained decoding up to 100x over prior solutions and reports near-zero end-to-end overhead when overlapped with GPU execution. Outlines / 'Efficient Guided Generation for LLMs' (Willard & Louf, arXiv:2307.09702, Jul 2023) introduces the finite-state-machine indexing approach that adds little overhead and underpins jump-forward decoding. The 40-150 microsecond mask-overhead band and the 1.6x jump-forward speedup are guide-friendly approximations: the XGrammar paper reports sub-100 microsecond-class per-token mask costs in typical cases with much larger gains on complex grammars, and jump-forward gains depend on schema structure, being largest for JSON/function-call outputs. Treat both as illustrative, not exact published constants.

cold_start.source: Stage breakdown is a guide-friendly decomposition of a Kubernetes/vLLM container cold start summing to the 40-90 s baseline cited in the plan; individual stage times vary with image size, host CPU, storage and GPU. Weights: NVIDIA Run:ai Model Streamer (open source, github.com/run-ai/runai-model-streamer; benchmarks doc and NVIDIA developer blog 'Reducing Cold Start Latency for LLM Inference with NVIDIA Run:ai Model Streamer', 16 Sep 2025) measured 43.71 s at concurrency 1 dropping to 7.53 s at concurrency 8 for a 15 GB Llama 3 8B model on IO2 SSD (-5.8x). baselineS 40 and improvedS 8 are rounded from that documented 43.7 s -> 7.5 s result; absolute times scale with model size and storage throughput.

engines.source: Project documentation and papers, retrieved 2026-09. vLLM (PagedAttention, Kwon et al., SOSP 2023, arXiv:2309.06180; docs.vllm.ai): paged KV cache, continuous batching, prefix caching, speculative decoding, LoRA, and disaggregated prefill/decode via connectors. SGLang (Zheng et al., arXiv:2312.07104; docs.sglang.ai): RadixAttention prefix cache, continuous batching, EAGLE speculative decoding, LoRA, and PD disaggregation. NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM (github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM docs): paged KV cache, in-flight batching, prefix caching, draft-model/Medusa/EAGLE speculative decoding, LoRA, and disaggregated serving. llama.cpp (github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp server docs): no paged attention, continuous batching via --cont-batching, prompt/KV cache reuse, speculative decoding (draft model and lookup), and LoRA adapters; no first-class prefill/decode disaggregation. Booleans indicate documented first-class support, not that every combination is production-ready.

items.name: vLLM
items.notes: PagedAttention origin; disaggregated prefill/decode via the vLLM disaggregation connectors; broad speculative-decoding support including n-gram and draft models.

items.name: SGLang
items.notes: RadixAttention prefix tree; strong EAGLE/EAGLE-3 speculative decoding and structured-output (XGrammar) integration.

items.name: TensorRT-LLM
items.notes: NVIDIA-optimized for Hopper/Blackwell; in-flight batching; FP8/FP4 and paged KV cache; disaggregated serving supported.

items.name: llama.cpp
items.notes: CPU/Metal/consumer-GPU focus; continuous batching via the server (--cont-batching); KV-cache/prompt reuse and draft-model/lookup speculative decoding; no paged attention or full PD disaggregation.

pricing.source: HISTORICAL vendor list prices, early-to-mid 2025, per 1M tokens (USD, standard, non-batch, USD). These rot fast and several models are now superseded or repriced; values are included as clearly labelled historical reference points, not current quotes. OpenAI GPT-4o and GPT-4o mini pricing pages (2024-2025); Anthropic Claude 3.5 Sonnet (2024) and Claude 3.7 Sonnet (Feb 2025) at $3/$15 with cache read $0.30; Google Gemini 1.5 Flash and Gemini 2.0 Flash pricing pages (2024-2025); DeepSeek-V3 official API pricing as of Feb 2025 ($0.07 cache hit / $0.27 cache miss / $1.10 output). DeepSeek's own open-infra note (2025-02-28) quotes the higher R1 rates ($0.14/$0.55/$2.19) and V3 is lower, so the V3 figure here is the mainstream one. Verify against the live vendor pricing pages before relying on any number.
